summary: This memo is an official ICCB and DARPA policy statement on rolling out the Exterior Gateway Protocol. After 1 August 1984 every gateway had to belong to an autonomous system, and some gateway of each system had to exchange routing information with the core using EGP.

plainLanguage.summary: The bosses of the network announced a deadline: after a set date, every router must join a team and talk to the main team using one shared language.

questions: when was egp required on the internet
policy on exterior gateway protocol rollout
subtitle: Official policy requiring all Internet gateways to implement the Exterior Gateway Protocol by August 1, 1984

tldr.problem: The current Internet routing system used GGP (Gateway-Gateway Protocol) on smart gateways while dumb gateways were manually configured. This approach was reaching capacity and prevented flexible routing architecture changes.
tldr.mechanism: The policy mandates that all dumb gateways be upgraded to stub EGP gateways and that smart gateways be organized into autonomous systems. Each autonomous system will use EGP to exchange routing information with other systems, creating a modular, scalable architecture.
tldr.outcome: After August 1, 1984, every Internet gateway must belong to an autonomous system and exchange routing with the core via EGP, replacing the flat smart/dumb model with a hierarchical structure that could scale better.

today: RFC 890 is an Unknown status policy statement from February 1984. EGP was succeeded by BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) as the standard exterior routing protocol, which provides greater expressiveness and flexibility for inter-domain routing.

sections.title: The Current Routing Problem
sections.content:
The Internet has two kinds of gateways: smart gateways that dynamically exchange routing information using GGP, and dumb gateways that are manually configured. Dumb gateways must be hand-entered into routing tables, and any change requires human intervention.

The current GGP system is at capacity limits. Gateways maintained by different groups cannot easily adopt improved routing procedures because any change must be coordinated across all smart gateways simultaneously. This architecture prevents the flexibility needed for network growth.
sections.plainLanguage: Some routers talked to each other automatically, but new ones were configured by hand. The automatic system was so full it could not grow anymore.

sections.title: The Future Model: Autonomous Systems
sections.content:
The solution divides the Internet into autonomous systems (ASes), each with its own internal routing procedures via an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP). Different autonomous systems can use different IGPs. The systems communicate externally using the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP).

This three-step transition plan: first, upgrade all dumb gateways to implement stub EGP; second, partition existing smart gateways into autonomous systems with a core system and several stub systems attached via EGP; third, complete the EGP protocol and allow rich connectivity between co-equal autonomous systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Split the network into teams. Each team manages its own internal routing. Teams talk to each other using one standard language (EGP). Different teams can use different internal methods.

sections.title: The Mandate
sections.content:
The RFC contains an official ICCB and DARPA policy statement: after 1 August 1984, there shall be no dumb gateways in the Internet. Every gateway must be a member of an autonomous system, and some gateway of each system must exchange routing information with the core autonomous system using EGP.

Implementation help is available from BBN, MIT, Linkabit, ISI, Honeywell, and Symbolics. A mailing list called egp-people coordinates implementers, and Berkeley's 4.2 Unix is planned to include EGP capability. An EGP testing program is available on TOPS-20.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the official rule. By August 1984, all routers must be updated. Help is available. After that date, every router follows the new system.
